en.title: Will Poulter Dives Deep into Recovery in 'Union County,' Earning Sundance Applause
en.summary: Will Poulter sheds his usual charisma for a raw, transformative performance in Adam Meeks' 'Union County.' The film, which premiered to a standing ovation at Sundance, offers a stark look at the arduous journey of addiction recovery.
en.body:
Few actors can command a room quite like **Will Poulter**. His striking looks and magnetic presence have often made him the focal point, even in supporting roles. However, in **Adam Meeks’** feature debut, **Union County**, Poulter undertakes a profound disappearing act. As Cody Parsons, a man battling heroin and alcohol addiction, he arrives at a courthouse stripped of his usual polish, sporting a scraggy beard and slumped shoulders. This deliberate unremarkability is the first step in a challenging, court-mandated journey toward sobriety.

Adapted from Meeks’ 2020 short film, **Union County** plunges viewers into the heart of rural Ohio’s opioid epidemic. The narrative follows Cody through the initial, often humbling, stages of a drug court program, a more hopeful alternative to incarceration. Under the guidance of a supportive counselor and facing regular drug tests and judicial check-ins, Cody, alongside his foster brother Jack (played by **Noah Centineo**, who also undergoes a significant physical transformation), grapples with regaining control of his life. What sets **Union County** apart is Meeks’ bold decision to integrate non-professional actors—individuals who are genuinely in recovery—alongside local figures like a judge. This powerful fusion of fiction and documentary aims for a potent, unflinching authenticity, illuminating the lives of those on society's margins as they strive for a second chance.

## The Unvarnished Truth of Recovery

The film’s strength lies in its commitment to depicting the slow, often unglamorous work of recovery. Unlike many cinematic portrayals that rush through rehabilitation, **Union County** embraces the day-to-day struggles, the setbacks, and the small victories. Meeks, who has spoken about his dedication to portraying his community with empathy, crafts a narrative that feels lived-in and true. The performances, particularly Poulter's, are lauded for their subdued yet compelling nature. Critics have noted that despite a seemingly predictable story arc, the film resonates deeply due to the genuine performances and Meeks’ sensitive direction.

## A Community's Standout Moment

**Union County** has already made a significant impact, earning a standing ovation at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival. The film's premiere, attended by Poulter and Meeks, highlighted its status as one of the festival's most talked-about features. The enthusiastic reception underscores the importance of such stories being told with honesty and compassion. For fans of cinema that tackles difficult subjects with nuance and respect, **Union County** represents a powerful testament to the resilience of the human spirit and a compelling showcase for **Will Poulter**'s dramatic range.

## What's Next

Following its acclaimed Sundance debut, **Union County** is set to open in theaters on August 14. Audiences can anticipate a film that is both a character study and a vital social commentary, promising a moving and authentic look at the path to healing.

content_raw: Note: This review was originally published as part of our 2026 Sundance coverage. The film opens on August 14. Last summer, in the middle of  The Bear ’s fourth season, Will Poulter strolled into the show’s eponymous Chicago restaurant and placed the kitchen staff’s jaws on the floor with his handsomeness. This wasn’t exactly a new reaction for the tall British actor—over the last few years, his cool, blue eyes, angular frame, and disarming accent have made him used to being looked at. No matter the supporting role, when he walks into a room, the energy changes. But in  Union County , writer-director Adam Meeks’ assured feature debut, Poulter tries a disappearing act. As recovering drug addict Cody Parsons, he trudges into a courthouse with a scraggy beard, unkempt hair, and slumped shoulders, sanding down his vibrant sheen into a pale matte. Nobody around him turns their head, let alone loosens their jaw.  The stripped-down look is a bid to blend in. Adapted from Meeks’ eponymous 2020 short film,  Union County  follows Cody through the first phase of a rural Ohio county-mandated drug court program (a more promising rehabilitation than short-term jail-sentencing) in the midst of the opioid epidemic. He works toward sobriety with his foster brother Jack (Noah Centineo, another handsome star scruffing up his face), struggling to regain control over heroin and alcohol with a supportive counselor, regular drug tests, and court check-ins in front of a judge. But unlike most movies about addiction, Meeks furnishes the pair’s journey with non-professional actors—a community of real addicts in recovery along with a local judge, merging fiction and documentary to achieve a more potent, authentic portrayal of people on society’s periphery, striving for sobriety and a new purpose.  Such filmmaking decisions can lead to accusations of exploitation—a kind of queasiness built around the idea that the real people of Bellefontaine, Ohio, will look like props, stripped of the same humanity and dignity as the professional actors attempting to become them. But Meeks mostly acquits those charges through his generosity and keen interest in the program’s process. He begins with testimony from recovering addicts and later documents group meetings where they can share their histories, tendencies, and encouragement. Meeks, a Brooklyn-based NYU film student from Columbus who spent most of his upbringing throughout central Ohio, saw the impact of the opioid crisis first-hand and has continued what he calls a “collaborative creative practice” within the community, becoming friends with program participants and court employees. The care and attention, visible in the tapestry of faces and voices, also seeps through depictions of the county’s environment, a bleak collage of empty roads and gray, bucolic vistas that only emphasize how vital human connection is to making daily progress.  Even with a dense backdrop and textured surroundings,&nbs
